In recent years, Foundation models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) have demonstrated strong generalization capabilities, but because they are primarily pre-trained on natural images, they perform poorly when faced with medical images. With sufficient labeled medical data, this challenge is somewhat alleviated. item.title: Foundation Model and Radiomics Distance Scores for Post-Hoc Segmentation Failure Detection
item.description:
arXiv Query: search_query=all:"foundation model" AND all:medical AND all:segmen… · score 0.52

Medical image segmentation models can fail silently when clinical data differs from training data. Deployed models rarely ship with quality control, and are often black boxes. Prior methods that work in this post-hoc failure detection setting still need a separate regression or segmentation model, registration, or access to model internals. We instead propose two failure scores based on the Mahalanobis distance to a labeled reference set. The first uses radiomic shape features of the predicted mask. item.title: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
Segment Anything In-Context via Visual Demonstrations
item.description:
arXiv Query: search_query=all:"foundation model" AND all:medical AND all:segmen… · score 0.43

We present the Segment Anything Model via Visual Demonstrations (SAYD), a foundation model for in-context segmentation. Given visual demos comprising prompt images and their segmentation masks, SAYD segments coherent regions (e.g., objects or their parts) in a query image by establishing visual correspondences between the prompts and the query. SAYD generalizes to previously-unseen segmentation tasks, including those requiring tacit visual knowledge or involving concepts that are difficult to articulate unambiguously in language. item.title: GeoSurge: Geometry-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning for Auditable Liver Resection Planning
item.description:
arXiv Query: search_query=all:"foundation model" AND all:medical AND all:segmen… · score 0.41

Surgical resection planning centers on generating executable resection surfaces from anatomical evidence and operative constraints. Medical multimodal foundation models enable anatomical understanding, and segmentation models predict resection regions, but neither translates these capabilities into explicitly constrained, executable resection surfaces. We present GeoSurge, an anatomy-grounded framework that combines mask-derived metrics with structure-aware point-cloud tokens to generate executable, editable resection surfaces.
